newsitem.title: RUSSIA: EU praises reforms as Yeltsin continues comeback.
newsitem.headline: EU praises reforms as Yeltsin continues comeback.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, taking a further step in his comeback after illness, met European Union leaders on Monday and won their praise over reforms at the start of a week that could bring a government reshuffle.

Yeltsin told European Commission President Jacques Santer and Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok, whose country holds the EU's rotating presidency, that he was pleased with Russian-EU relations and they were vital for Europe's security.
Kok responded in a similarly positive vein after meeting Yeltsin in the Kremlin.

"Of course problems remain, but Russia is on the right track (of economic reforms)," Kok told a news conference. "It is clear that Russia and the European Union need each other and have the political will to cooperate."
The Kremlin said in a statement that agreement was reached in principle on a permanent mechanism to deal with economic, trade, scientific and cultural issues between Russia and the EU.
The Russian side pressed demands for more access to European markets -- something EU companies fear could unleash a flood of cheap imports.
Yeltsin also repeated Moscow's opposition to NATO's plans to offer membership to some former Soviet-bloc states in eastern and central Europe.
NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana visits Moscow this weekend in a new effort to soothe Russian fears over expansion and an aide is due in Moscow on Tuesday to prepare the visit.
Russian deputy foreign minister Nikolai Afanasevsky told Interfax news agency that Moscow expected him to bring "constructive" proposals.
Russia regards NATO's enlargement as a threat to its own security and wants a legally binding treaty with the alliance to safeguard its interests.
Moscow and NATO hope to reach agreement before an alliance summit in Madrid in July at which the first new membership invitations are to be issued.
"The Russian attitude has not changed (from opposing NATO expansion) but at the same time there is a strong will to reach a set of conclusions before Madrid," Kok said.

Yeltsin's EU summit was originally scheduled for February 4 in The Hague but was postponed when the president came down with pneumonia in January after a brief return to the Kremlin following his November heart bypass operation.
Yeltsin was now "in excellent spirits, a creative, active negotiating partner", Kok said.

Clearly determined to stamp his authority after spending most of the first eight months of his second term out of action, Yeltsin has criticised Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin's budget and demanded a reshuffle.

Government changes are expected to be announced after Yeltsin faces his biggest physical test in public since his re-election campaign when he gives a 40-minute state of the nation address to parliament on Thursday.
Some news media have speculated Chernomyrdin could be dismissed but many analysts say he will stay on.

Deputy Communist party leader Valentin Kuptsov told the party's Central Committee that patience with the government was running out and it could face a no-confidence motion next month in the opposition-dominated State Duma lower house.
Kuptsov said Chernomyrdin had reneged on promises to pay out wage and pension arrears which he had made in order to secure communist backing for the government's 1997 budget.
